claims.evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of proteomic data (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils include GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN.
claims.source: Among these, we found known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils, such as GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN (Sachs et al., 2007), as well as ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase SHIP1 (Pumphrey et al., 1999), and integrins such as CD11b and CD18 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by proteomic data and cited previous studies (Sachs et al., 2007) (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: SHIP1 is an ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase that associates with CD31.
claims.source: Among these, we found known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils, such as GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN (Sachs et al., 2007), as well as ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase SHIP1 (Pumphrey et al., 1999), and integrins such as CD11b and CD18 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by proteomic data and cited previous study (Pumphrey et al., 1999) (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: Integrins such as CD11b and CD18 associate with CD31.
claims.source: Among these, we found known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils, such as GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN (Sachs et al., 2007), as well as ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase SHIP1 (Pumphrey et al., 1999), and integrins such as CD11b and CD18 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by proteomic data showing CD11b and CD18 in CD31 immunoprecipitates (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: The CD31 interactome was linked to the integrin and actin networks, under resting and activated conditions.
claims.source: Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) and KEGG functional annotation pathways revealed that the CD31 interactome was linked to the integrin and actin networks, under resting and activated conditions, consistent with the role of CD31 in neutrophil migration (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by IPA and KEGG pathway analysis of proteomic data (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).

claims.claim: CD31, through SHIP1 (INDPP5), regulates cytoskeleton reorganization and integrin activation during neutrophil migration.
claims.source: Based on the IPA results, we elaborated a model of protein interaction showing how CD31, through SHIP1 (INDPP5), regulates cytoskeleton reorganization and integrin activation during neutrophil migration (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Inferred from IPA network analysis of CD31 interactome showing connections between CD31, SHIP1, and cytoskeletal/integrin proteins (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: Both CD31 and CD11b rapidly relocated to the uropod during neutrophil migration.
claims.source: We found that both CD31 and CD11b rapidly relocated to the uropod during neutrophil migration (Figure 2F and G and Video 1), while a minor fraction of both molecules remained localized at the leading edge.
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging microscopy showing CD31 and CD11b localization at the uropod (Figure 2F and G and Video 1).

claims.claim: A minor fraction of CD31 and CD11b remained localized at the leading edge during neutrophil migration.
claims.source: We found that both CD31 and CD11b rapidly relocated to the uropod during neutrophil migration (Figure 2F and G and Video 1), while a minor fraction of both molecules remained localized at the leading edge.
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging microscopy showing some CD31 and CD11b at the leading edge (Figure 2F and G).

claims.claim: CD31 localizes preferentially to the uropod in human neutrophils interacting with immobilized ICAM-1 and IL-8.
claims.source: Under these conditions, we found that CD31 localizes preferentially to the uropod and, only at the rear, CD31 displayed phosphorylated ITIM motifs (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing CD31 localization at the uropod (Figure 2H).

claims.claim: Only at the rear of neutrophils, CD31 displayed phosphorylated ITIM motifs.
claims.source: Under these conditions, we found that CD31 localizes preferentially to the uropod and, only at the rear, CD31 displayed phosphorylated ITIM motifs (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing pY713 staining at the uropod (Figure 2H).

claims.claim: SHIP1 was concentrated at the cellular rear of migrating neutrophils.
claims.source: In addition, SH2-containing inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which has been found in the CD31 interactome, was also concentrated at the cellular rear (Figure 2I), supporting the notion that functional CD31 molecular clusters are present in the uropods of motile neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing SHIP-1 localization at the uropod (Figure 2I).

claims.claim: Functional CD31 molecular clusters are present in the uropods of motile neutrophils.
claims.source: In addition, SH2-containing inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which has been found in the CD31 interactome, was also concentrated at the cellular rear (Figure 2I), supporting the notion that functional CD31 molecular clusters are present in the uropods of motile neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the co-localization of CD31, phosphorylated CD31 (pY713), and SHIP1 at the uropod (Figure 2H, 2I).

claims.claim: Clusters positive for NKI-L16 (indicating active integrins) were exclusively localized at the leading edge, where CD31 was absent.
claims.source: Clusters positive for NKI-L16 (indicating active integrins, shown in red) were exclusively localized at the leading edge, where CD31 (shown in green) was absent.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing mutually exclusive distribution of NKI-L16 and CD31 (Figure 2J).

claims.claim: The staining with NKI-L16 antibody was absent at the uropod, where most CD31 was concentrated.
claims.source: Conversely, the staining with this antibody was absent at the uropod, where most CD31 was concentrated (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing absence of NKI-L16 staining at the uropod where CD31 is concentrated (Figure 2J).

claims.claim: CD31 is enriched at the uropod along with closed β2-integrins, in contrast to fully opened integrins that are restricted to the leading edge.
claims.source: The co-localization of functional CD31 clusters with integrins that did not react with the NKI-L16 antibody indicates that CD31 is enriched at the uropod along with closed β2-integrins, in contrast to fully opened integrins that are restricted to the leading edge.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 co-localizes with total CD11a but not with NKI-L16-positive (active) CD11a at the uropod (Figure 2J).

claims.claim: CD31 signaling may contribute to maintaining integrins in a closed/bent conformation at the uropod during neutrophil migration.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings suggest that CD31 signaling may contribute to maintaining integrins in a closed/bent conformation at the uropod, the region where cell detachment is required, during neutrophil migration.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the co-localization of CD31 with closed integrins at the uropod and the absence of active integrins in this region (Figure 2J).

claims.claim: Wild-type neutrophils quickly polarized with a leading-edge rich in F-actin, while the integrin-associated protein talin accumulated at the uropod.
claims.source: In agreement with previous studies (Pouwels et al., 2013), wild-type neutrophils quickly polarized with a leading-edge rich in F-actin, while the integrin-associated protein talin accumulated at the uropod, where the location of the two proteins was almost mutually exclusive (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing F-actin at the front and talin at the back of WT neutrophils (Figure 3A and B).

claims.claim: The location of F-actin and talin was almost mutually exclusive in wild-type neutrophils.
claims.source: In agreement with previous studies (Pouwels et al., 2013), wild-type neutrophils quickly polarized with a leading-edge rich in F-actin, while the integrin-associated protein talin accumulated at the uropod, where the location of the two proteins was almost mutually exclusive (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing spatial separation of F-actin and talin in WT neutrophils (Figure 3A and B).

claims.claim: Talin was spatially far from F-actin at the cell rear in WT leukocytes, indicating that the integrins at the uropod were in a low-adhesive conformation state.
claims.source: The fact that talin was spatially far from F-actin at the cell rear indicated that the integrins at the uropod of WT leukocytes were in a low-adhesive conformation state.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that talin and F-actin are spatially separated at the uropod, and talin is known to bridge cytoskeleton and active integrins (Figure 3A and B).

claims.claim: Polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear.
claims.source: Instead, such polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear (Figure 3C) so that Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D and E), thus reflecting an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing co-localization of F-actin and talin at the rear of Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3C).

claims.claim: Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells.
claims.source: Instead, such polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear (Figure 3C) so that Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D and E), thus reflecting an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification showing significantly longer uropods and larger cell area in Pecam1-/- neutrophils compared to WT (Figure 3D and E).

claims.claim: Pecam1-/- neutrophils reflect an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
claims.source: Instead, such polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear (Figure 3C) so that Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D and E), thus reflecting an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the defective polarization, elongated uropods, and abnormal distribution of F-actin and talin in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3C-E).

claims.claim: In wild-type neutrophils, SHIP1 was preferentially localized together with CD44 at the site of a clearly identifiable uropod.
claims.source: Whereas in wild-type neutrophils SHIP1 was preferentially localized together with CD44 at the site of a clearly identifiable uropod (Figure 3F), CD44 and SHIP1 were both distributed more evenly throughout the cell body in Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing co-localization of SHIP1 and CD44 at the uropod in WT neutrophils (Figure 3F).

claims.claim: CD44 and SHIP1 were both distributed more evenly throughout the cell body in Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
claims.source: Whereas in wild-type neutrophils SHIP1 was preferentially localized together with CD44 at the site of a clearly identifiable uropod (Figure 3F), CD44 and SHIP1 were both distributed more evenly throughout the cell body in Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing diffuse distribution of SHIP1 and CD44 in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3G).

claims.claim: CD31 was critically involved in uropod formation of neutrophils interacting with laminin.
claims.source: These findings further supported the hypothesis that CD31 was critically involved in uropod formation of neutrophils interacting with laminin.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pecam1-/- neutrophils show defective uropod formation and abnormal distribution of uropod markers (Figure 3F-G).

claims.claim: Experiments performed with Pecam1ITIM-/- mice phenocopied the data obtained using whole Pecam1-/- deficiency.
claims.source: Experiments performed with these mice phenocopied the data obtained using whole Pecam1-/- deficiency (Figure 3H–K), demonstrating that CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing similar defects in Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils as in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3H-K).

claims.claim: CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
claims.source: Experiments performed with these mice phenocopied the data obtained using whole Pecam1-/- deficiency (Figure 3H–K), demonstrating that CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that deletion of CD31 ITIM motifs produces the same phenotype as complete CD31 deletion (Figure 3H-K).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist P8RI effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in T lymphocytes.
claims.source: In our previous studies, we demonstrated that P8RI, a CD31 agonist peptide, effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in T lymphocytes (Clement et al., 2015; Fornasa et al., 2012; Fornasa et al., 2010) and macrophages (Andreata et al., 2018), thereby providing promising potential for theranostic applications (Hoang et al., 2018; Vigne et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Clement et al., 2015; Fornasa et al., 2012; Fornasa et al., 2010).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist P8RI effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in macrophages.
claims.source: In our previous studies, we demonstrated that P8RI, a CD31 agonist peptide, effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in T lymphocytes (Clement et al., 2015; Fornasa et al., 2012; Fornasa et al., 2010) and macrophages (Andreata et al., 2018), thereby providing promising potential for theranostic applications (Hoang et al., 2018; Vigne et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous study (Andreata et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation during fMLP activation in neutrophils.
claims.source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot showing increased CD31 pY713 with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 clustering during fMLP activation in neutrophils.
claims.source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy showing increased CD31 clustering with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist specifically targets the CD31 molecule in neutrophils.
claims.source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing CD31 agonist binding only to WT but not Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist fine-tunes cytoskeleton dynamics in neutrophils.
claims.source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing altered actin polymerization kinetics with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claims.claim: 1 hr after intradermal IL-1β injection, Lyz2-GFP+ cells exhibited crawling behavior along the post-capillary blood vessels.
claims.source: Our observations revealed that 1 hr after intradermal IL-1β injection, Lyz2-GFP+ cells exhibited crawling behavior along the post-capillary blood vessels.
claims.evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy observations of Lyz2-GFP+ cells in vivo (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: Extravasating leukocytes demonstrated delayed uropod detachment and underwent significant elongation before being disconnected from the basement membrane.
claims.source: Extravasating leukocytes demonstrated delayed uropod detachment and underwent significant elongation before being disconnected from the basement membrane (Figure 4A and B and Video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy images showing elongated cells during extravasation (Figure 4A and B and Video 2).

claims.claim: Administration of the CD31 agonist 1 hr after the initiation of Lyz2-GFP+ cell extravasation resulted in a remarkable acceleration of uropod detachment from the basement membrane.
claims.source: Administration of the CD31 agonist 1 hr after the initiation of Lyz2-GFP+ cell extravasation resulted in a remarkable acceleration of uropod detachment from the basement membrane.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification showing significantly faster detachment speed with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist led to an increased migratory capacity of Lyz2-GFP+ cells in the extravascular space compared to cells from vehicle-treated mice.
claims.source: This led to an increased migratory capacity of Lyz2-GFP+ cells in the extravascular space compared to cells from vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4A and B and Video 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy images and quantification showing increased migration with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4A-C).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist enhanced the migratory capacity of extravasated Lyz2-GFP+ cells 3 hr after inducing inflammation in the extravascular space.
claims.source: Furthermore, our investigation of the fate of extravasated Lyz2-GFP+ cells 3 hr after inducing inflammation revealed that the CD31 agonist enhanced their migratory capacity in the extravascular space (Figure 4C and D and Videos 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy images and quantification showing enhanced migration at 3 hr with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4C-H).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist enhanced neutrophil migration as demonstrated by increased speed, shorter cellular length, and greater traveling distance compared to the control group.
claims.source: This enhancement was demonstrated by increased speed, shorter cellular length, and greater traveling distance compared to the control group (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of speed, length, circularity, and track plots showing enhanced migration with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4E-H).

claims.claim: CD31 signaling actively participates in uropod detachment from the vessel after neutrophil transendothelial migration outside the vessel wall.
claims.source: Taken together, these gain-of-function experiments provided further evidence that CD31 signaling actively participates in uropod detachment from the vessel after neutrophil transendothelial migration outside the vessel wall.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that enhancing CD31 signaling with the agonist accelerates uropod detachment and improves migration (Figure 4A-H).

claims.claim: In WT mice, RGD peptides did not modify IL-1β-induced neutrophil accumulation in the peritoneal cavity.
claims.source: In WT mice, RGD peptides did not modify IL-1β-induced neutrophil accumulation in the peritoneal cavity (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing no significant difference in neutrophil numbers with RGD treatment in WT mice (Figure 5B and C).

claims.claim: Extravascular (i.p.) injection of RGD peptides rescued the defective neutrophil accumulation in Pecam1-/- mice upon IL-1β-induced peritonitis.
claims.source: However, extravascular (i.p.) injection of RGD peptides rescued the defective neutrophil accumulation in Pecam1-/- mice upon IL-1β-induced peritonitis (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophil numbers with RGD treatment in Pecam1-/- mice (Figure 5B and C).

claims.claim: RGD injection enhanced extravascular detachment of Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
claims.source: Corresponding fluorescent microscopy analysis confirmed the enhanced extravascular detachment of Pecam1-/- neutrophils upon RGD injection (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing increased distance of Pecam1-/- neutrophils from vessels with RGD treatment (Figure 5D and E).

claims.claim: The CD31 agonist increased neutrophil recruitment into the peritoneal cavity.
claims.source: Based on the observation that the CD31 agonist increased neutrophil recruitment into the peritoneal cavity (Figure 5F–H), we investigated whether CD31 intracellular signaling, rather than its ectodomain properties, plays a role in regulating the recruitment of neutrophils to the site of inflammation.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophil numbers with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 5F-H).

claims.claim: Despite equal frequencies of WT and Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils in the blood before and after IL-1β injection, Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils exhibited a disadvantage in recruitment into the inflamed peritoneum compared to their WT counterparts.
claims.source: Despite equal frequencies of WT and Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils (identified by flow cytometry as CD45+ Ly6G+) in the blood before and after IL-1β injection (Figure 5J and K), Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils exhibited a disadvantage in recruitment into the inflamed peritoneum compared to their WT counterparts.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing equal frequencies in blood but reduced recruitment of Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils to peritoneum (Figure 5J-L).

claims.claim: The CD31 ITIM-dependent intracellular pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating neutrophil migration within the extravascular space during inflammation.
claims.source: In summary, our collective findings provide compelling evidence that the CD31 ITIM-dependent intracellular pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating neutrophil migration within the extravascular space during inflammation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that deletion of CD31 ITIM motifs impairs neutrophil recruitment to inflammatory sites (Figure 5I-L).

claims.claim: CD31 ITIM-dependent pathway effectively controls integrin activation at the uropod.
claims.source: Specifically, it effectively controls integrin activation at the uropod, thereby exerting a significant influence on the efficient movement of neutrophils.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 co-localizes with closed integrins at the uropod and its absence leads to defective uropod detachment (Figure 2J, Figure 3, Figure 5).

claims.claim: CD31 regulatory mechanism ensures the timely arrival of neutrophils at the inflammatory site, facilitating their efficient migration and precise targeting of the inflamed area.
claims.source: This regulatory mechanism ensures the timely arrival of neutrophils at the inflammatory site, facilitating their efficient migration and precise targeting of the inflamed area, thereby optimizing the immune response.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 deficiency or ITIM deletion delays neutrophil arrival at inflammatory sites (Figure 1, Figure 5).

claims.claim: CD31 signaling at the uropod plays a key role in the polarization and detachment of neutrophils.
claims.source: We found that CD31 signaling at the uropod plays a key role in the polarization and detachment of neutrophils, which is crucial for initiating their migration within the vascular compartment and subsequent progression through the interstitial tissue following extravasation towards inflammatory sites.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 localizes to the uropod, its absence causes defective polarization and detachment, and enhancing its signaling improves these processes (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).

claims.claim: The uropod remains trapped at the basolateral membrane of endothelial cell junctions, while the leading edge moves forward in the interstitial tissue.
claims.source: Our observations confirmed the dynamic behavior of neutrophils, wherein the uropod remains trapped at the basolateral membrane of endothelial cell junctions, while the leading edge moves forward in the interstitial tissue (Hind et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous study (Hind et al., 2016) and confirmed by observations in this study.

claims.claim: The detachment of the uropod is a crucial process that enables neutrophils to transition from a firmly adhesive state within blood vessels to a rapidly migratory configuration in the static extravascular space.
claims.source: The detachment of the uropod is a crucial process that enables neutrophils to transition from a firmly adhesive state within blood vessels, under strong hemodynamic conditions, to a rapidly migratory configuration in the static extravascular space.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that neutrophils must detach from the vessel wall to migrate effectively in the extravascular space (Figure 1, Figure 4).

claims.claim: The administration of soluble RGD peptides in the extravascular space effectively rescued the stagnation of Pecam1-/- neutrophils within the extracellular matrix.
claims.source: Nevertheless, our data unequivocally demonstrated that the administration of soluble RGD peptides in the extravascular space effectively rescued the stagnation of Pecam1-/- neutrophils within the extracellular matrix.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and microscopy data showing increased neutrophil detachment and recruitment with RGD treatment in Pecam1-/- mice (Figure 5B-E).

claims.claim: RGD peptides competitively bind to the RDG motif found in various extracellular matrix proteins, potentially reversing the excessive adhesion of RGD-binding β1 integrins.
claims.source: These peptides competitively bind to the RDG motif found in various extracellular matrix proteins, potentially reversing the excessive adhesion of RGD-binding β1 integrins and facilitating proper neutrophil migration toward sites of inflammation.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of RGD peptide function and inferred from the rescue of Pecam1-/- neutrophil migration by RGD treatment (Figure 5).

claims.claim: The retention of Pecam1-/- neutrophils in the extravascular interstitium is primarily due to the excessive adhesion of integrins to the components of the extracellular matrix.
claims.source: Therefore, our data strongly suggest that the retention of Pecam1-/- neutrophils in the extravascular interstitium is primarily due to the excessive adhesion of integrins to the components of the extracellular matrix.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking integrin-ECM interactions with RGD peptides rescues the migration defect in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Previous studies have proposed that impaired CD31-dependent upregulation of β1-integrin leads to the inability of Pecam1-/- neutrophils to exit blood vessels.
claims.source: Previous studies have proposed that impaired CD31-dependent upregulation of β1-integrin leads to the inability of Pecam1-/- neutrophils to exit blood vessels (Dangerfield et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous study (Dangerfield et al., 2002).

claims.claim: Recent evidence demonstrates that neutrophils lacking β1-integrins actually have an enhanced ability to reach inflamed sites.
claims.source: However, recent evidence challenges this hypothesis by demonstrating that neutrophils lacking β1-integrins actually have an enhanced ability to reach inflamed sites (Sarangi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous study (Sarangi et al., 2012).

claims.claim: CD31 may be involved in β1-integrin conformation rather than solely regulating its expression.
claims.source: Our present findings suggest that CD31 may be involved in β1-integrin conformation rather than solely regulating its expression.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 co-localizes with closed integrins and RGD peptides rescue the migration defect (Figure 2J, Figure 5).

claims.claim: Proteomic analysis revealed that CD31 partners were also associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: While our primary focus was on investigating CD31's role in uropod detachment, proteomic analysis revealed that CD31 partners were also associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: Supported by IPA and KEGG pathway analysis showing enrichment of actin cytoskeleton-related proteins in CD31 interactome (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Both the presence of CD31 and its intact intracellular tail with the ITIM motifs are essential for proper functional cell polarization during neutrophil migration.
claims.source: This indicates that both the presence of CD31 and its intact intracellular tail with the ITIM motifs are essential for proper functional cell polarization during neutrophil migration.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that both Pecam1-/- and Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils show similar defects in polarization (Figure 3).

claims.claim: The polarization defect in CD31-deficient neutrophils could potentially impact the coordination between the leading edge and the uropod.
claims.source: This polarization defect could potentially impact the coordination between the leading edge and the uropod, which is crucial for effective neutrophil extravasation (Hind et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of defective polarization in CD31-deficient neutrophils and cited previous study (Hind et al., 2016).

claims.claim: After being phosphorylated by active co-clustered ITAM receptors, the ITIM motifs of CD31 act as docking sites for several proteins and lipid SH2-containing phosphatases.
claims.source: After being phosphorylated by active co-clustered ITAM receptors, the ITIM motifs of CD31 act as docking sites for several proteins (Henshall et al., 2001; Sagawa et al., 1997) and lipid SH2-containing phosphatases (Ilan and Madri, 2003, p. 1), which drive downstream signaling pathways upon CD31 engagement in various biological processes.
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Henshall et al., 2001; Sagawa et al., 1997; Ilan and Madri, 2003).

claims.claim: Previous studies have highlighted the significant involvement of lipid phosphatases in the regulation of leukocyte migration.
claims.source: Previous studies have highlighted the significant involvement of lipid phosphatases in the regulation of leukocyte migration (Michael et al., 2021; Mondal et al., 2012; Nishio et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Michael et al., 2021; Mondal et al., 2012; Nishio et al., 2007).

claims.claim: SHIP-1 acts as a critical mediator of CD31 signaling in integrin closure during neutrophil migration.
claims.source: Our data strongly suggest that SHIP-1 acts as a critical mediator of CD31 signaling in integrin closure during neutrophil migration.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that SHIP-1 is found in the CD31 interactome and co-localizes with CD31 at the uropod (Figure 2E, 2I, 3F).

claims.claim: The concentration of endothelial CD31 at lateral borders likely plays a crucial role in regulating the engagement of CD31 on neutrophils during transendothelial migration.
claims.source: The concentration of endothelial CD31 at lateral borders (Newman, 1994) likely plays a crucial role in regulating the engagement of CD31 on neutrophils during transendothelial migration.
claims.evidence: Inferred from cited previous study (Newman, 1994) and the observation that CD31 is involved in neutrophil extravasation.

claims.claim: CD31 undergoes rapid tyrosine phosphorylation in response to mechanical stress.
claims.source: Moreover, CD31 undergoes rapid tyrosine phosphorylation in response to mechanical stress (Masuda et al., 2004; Snyder et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies (Masuda et al., 2004; Snyder et al., 2017).

claims.claim: As neutrophils pass through the lateral endothelial cell junctions, CD31 may sense the gradient of mechanical forces generated within the cell across the vascular barrier.
claims.source: These findings suggest that, as neutrophils pass through the lateral endothelial cell junctions, CD31 may sense the gradient of mechanical forces generated within the cell across the vascular barrier.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 is phosphorylated during extravasation and is known to respond to mechanical stress (Figure 1E, cited studies).

claims.claim: The concentration of CD31 at the uropod may be required to 'free' this pole of the cell, allowing it to continue its journey toward the inflammatory site guided by chemokine gradients in the extravascular space.
claims.source: Based on our observations, we propose that the concentration of CD31 at the uropod may be required to 'free' this pole of the cell, allowing it to continue its journey toward the inflammatory site guided by chemokine gradients in the extravascular space.

results.result: CD31 deficiency impairs neutrophil detachment from the outer vessel wall after extravasation. In WT mice, neutrophils accumulate in the peritoneal cavity within 4 hr after IL-1β injection, with CD31 phosphorylation (pY713) inversely correlated with distance from the vessel wall. In Pecam1-/- mice, neutrophils extravasate but remain attached to the outer vessel wall, failing to reach the inflammatory site in a timely manner. This defect is not due to differences in blood neutrophil levels or inflammatory mediators.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 collectively demonstrate that CD31 is required for neutrophil detachment from the vessel wall after extravasation. The data show clear differences between WT and Pecam1-/- mice in neutrophil accumulation (C1-C2), spatial distribution (C5, C8-C9), and CD31 phosphorylation patterns (C6-C7), with appropriate controls for confounding factors (C4). The microscopy and flow cytometry data provide converging evidence for the proposed role of CD31 in uropod detachment.

results.result: CD31 interactome analysis reveals association with integrin and actin networks. Proteomic analysis identified 173 proteins co-immunoprecipitated with CD31 in human neutrophils, including known CD31 partners (GRB2, CD177, SHP, MSN), SHIP1, and integrins (CD11b, CD18). Pathway analysis linked the CD31 interactome to integrin and actin networks under both resting and activated conditions, suggesting CD31 regulates cytoskeleton reorganization and integrin activation through SHIP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C20 present proteomic data identifying CD31-associated proteins and pathway enrichment. While the mass spectrometry data (C12-C15) and identification of known partners (C16-C18) are supported, the study uses N=1 for each condition (duplicates only), which is insufficient for robust proteomic conclusions. The pathway analysis (C19) and proposed model (C20) are inferential and require functional validation. The lack of biological replicates and validation experiments limits confidence in these findings.

results.result: CD31 localizes to the uropod of migrating neutrophils along with closed integrins. Live imaging and confocal microscopy show that CD31 and CD11b relocate to the uropod during neutrophil migration, where CD31 displays phosphorylated ITIM motifs and co-localizes with SHIP1. Active integrins (NKI-L16-positive) are exclusively at the leading edge, while CD31 co-localizes with closed integrins at the uropod, suggesting CD31 maintains integrins in a closed conformation at the uropod.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C31 provide strong evidence for CD31 localization and function at the uropod. The live imaging (C21-C22), confocal microscopy (C24-C26), and integrin activation state analysis (C28-C30) are well-documented with appropriate quantification. The spatial segregation of CD31 with closed integrins versus active integrins at different cellular poles is clearly demonstrated. However, the mechanistic conclusion (C31) is inferential and would benefit from direct functional tests of integrin conformation.

results.result: CD31 deficiency causes defective neutrophil polarization with abnormal uropod organization. WT neutrophils show proper polarization with F-actin at the leading edge and talin at the uropod, spatially separated. Pecam1-/- neutrophils exhibit defective polarization with F-actin and talin co-localized at the rear, elongated uropods, and diffuse distribution of SHIP1 and CD44, indicating CD31 is critically involved in uropod formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C40 demonstrate clear morphological and organizational defects in Pecam1-/- neutrophils. The confocal microscopy data with quantification (C32-C36) show statistically significant differences in polarization, uropod length, and cell area. The altered distribution of uropod markers SHIP1 and CD44 (C38-C39) provides additional support. The conclusion that CD31 is involved in uropod formation (C40) is well-supported by the collective evidence, though the molecular mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: CD31 ITIM signaling motifs are required for proper neutrophil polarization. Experiments with Pecam1ITIM-/- mice (lacking ITIM motifs) phenocopy the defects observed in complete Pecam1-/- mice, demonstrating that CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 provide strong genetic evidence that CD31 signaling through ITIM motifs is essential for neutrophil polarization. The generation and characterization of Pecam1ITIM-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is well-documented, and the phenocopy of Pecam1-/- defects (C41) clearly demonstrates that the signaling function, not just the presence of CD31, is required. This is a key mechanistic finding that distinguishes signaling from structural roles.

results.result: CD31 agonist enhances neutrophil uropod detachment and migration in vivo. The CD31 agonist P8RI sustains CD31 phosphorylation, clustering, and fine-tunes cytoskeleton dynamics in neutrophils. In vivo two-photon microscopy shows that CD31 agonist administration accelerates uropod detachment from the basement membrane and enhances migratory capacity of extravasated neutrophils, with increased speed, shorter cellular length, and greater traveling distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C55 provide compelling gain-of-function evidence for CD31's role in uropod detachment. The in vitro characterization of the CD31 agonist (C45-C48) is supported by Western blot, TIRF microscopy, and flow cytometry data. The in vivo two-photon microscopy experiments (C49-C54) demonstrate clear functional effects on uropod detachment and migration with appropriate quantification. The data from two independent experiments with consistent results strengthen the conclusions. This represents strong functional validation of the proposed CD31 mechanism.

results.result: RGD peptides rescue neutrophil migration defects in Pecam1-/- mice by antagonizing integrin-ECM interactions. RGD peptides do not affect neutrophil accumulation in WT mice but rescue defective neutrophil accumulation and enhance extravascular detachment in Pecam1-/- mice. This suggests that retention of Pecam1-/- neutrophils is due to excessive integrin adhesion to ECM components.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58, C67-C69 provide strong evidence that integrin-ECM interactions underlie the Pecam1-/- phenotype. The rescue experiment is well-designed with appropriate controls (no effect in WT mice, C56), and the flow cytometry and microscopy data clearly show rescue of the migration defect (C57-C58). The interpretation that RGD peptides competitively inhibit integrin-ECM binding (C68) is based on established knowledge and supported by the functional rescue. This is a key mechanistic insight linking CD31 to integrin regulation.

results.result: CD31 ITIM-dependent signaling regulates neutrophil migration in the extravascular space. CD31 agonist increases neutrophil recruitment to the peritoneal cavity. In competitive adoptive transfer experiments, Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils show reduced recruitment to inflamed peritoneum compared to WT neutrophils despite equal frequencies in blood, demonstrating that CD31 ITIM-dependent signaling controls integrin activation at the uropod and ensures timely neutrophil arrival at inflammatory sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 provide strong evidence for the role of CD31 ITIM signaling in neutrophil recruitment. The CD31 agonist data (C59) and competitive adoptive transfer experiment (C60) are well-designed and clearly demonstrate a cell-intrinsic requirement for CD31 ITIM signaling. The equal frequencies in blood (C60) control for mobilization defects, and the reduced peritoneal recruitment specifically implicates extravascular migration. The conclusions about CD31 controlling integrin activation (C61-C63) are well-supported by the collective data from this and previous results.

results.result: CD31 acts as a molecular rheostat controlling integrin-mediated adhesion at the uropod. CD31 signaling at the uropod is crucial for neutrophil polarization and detachment, enabling transition from a firmly adhesive state in blood vessels to a rapidly migratory configuration in the extravascular space. CD31 may sense mechanical forces during extravasation and recruit phosphatases to its phosphorylated ITIMs, resulting in closed/inactive integrin conformation at the uropod, thereby triggering detachment from the outer vessel wall.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66, C82-C84, C97 present the overall model and mechanistic interpretation. While the functional role of CD31 in uropod detachment is well-supported by the experimental data, the proposed mechanism involving mechanical sensing (C81-C82) and phosphatase recruitment leading to integrin closure (C83) is largely speculative. The model is consistent with the data and prior knowledge about CD31 mechanosensing (C80), but direct evidence for mechanical force sensing, phosphatase recruitment, and causal effects on integrin conformation is lacking. The 'molecular rheostat' concept (C97) is a reasonable interpretation but requires further validation.

results.result: CD31 may regulate β1-integrin conformation rather than expression. Previous studies proposed that CD31 deficiency impairs β1-integrin upregulation, but recent evidence shows neutrophils lacking β1-integrins have enhanced ability to reach inflamed sites. The present findings suggest CD31 is involved in β1-integrin conformation rather than solely regulating expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 address conflicting prior literature and propose an alternative interpretation. While the citations to prior work (C70-C71) are appropriate, the conclusion that CD31 regulates integrin conformation (C72) is inferential and based primarily on the RGD rescue experiment and co-localization data. Direct measurement of integrin conformation states in WT versus Pecam1-/- neutrophils would be needed to definitively support this claim. The speculation is reasonable but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: CD31 and its ITIM motifs are essential for neutrophil polarization, potentially impacting coordination between leading edge and uropod. Proteomic analysis revealed CD31 partners associated with the actin cytoskeleton. Both CD31 presence and intact ITIM motifs are required for proper polarization, and this defect could impact coordination between cellular poles during extravasation.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 summarize findings about CD31's role in polarization. The proteomic data (C73) and genetic evidence from Pecam1-/- and Pecam1ITIM-/- mice (C74) support the conclusion that both CD31 presence and ITIM signaling are required. However, the speculation about coordination between leading edge and uropod (C75) is not directly tested and relies on inference from the polarization defects and cited literature. The core claims about polarization requirements are well-supported, but the mechanistic implications remain speculative.

results.result: CD31 ITIM motifs recruit phosphatases that may regulate neutrophil migration through mechanical sensing. CD31 ITIMs act as docking sites for SH2-containing phosphatases after phosphorylation. Lipid phosphatases are involved in leukocyte migration regulation. SHIP-1 may act as a critical mediator of CD31 signaling in integrin closure. CD31 is enriched at endothelial lateral borders and undergoes phosphorylation in response to mechanical stress, potentially sensing force gradients during extravasation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 present mechanistic hypotheses about CD31 signaling. While the general knowledge about ITIM function (C76) and lipid phosphatases in migration (C77) is well-established from cited literature, the specific role of SHIP-1 in CD31-mediated integrin closure (C78) is speculative based on co-localization data. The mechanical sensing hypothesis (C79-C81) is plausible given cited evidence for CD31 mechanosensing, but direct evidence for mechanical force sensing during neutrophil extravasation is lacking. These claims represent reasonable hypotheses requiring further experimental validation.

results.result: Background and context for neutrophil migration and CD31 function. These claims establish the scientific context, including the importance of neutrophil migration for immunity, the adhesion cascade, the role of integrins, the gap in knowledge about integrin detachment mechanisms, and prior observations about CD31 deficiency blocking transmigration at the outer vessel wall.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C124 provide background information and context from established scientific knowledge and prior literature. These claims are appropriately cited and represent accurate summaries of the field. They establish the rationale for the study by identifying the gap in knowledge about integrin detachment mechanisms (C89, C114) and the controversial cellular defects associated with CD31 deficiency (C91, C117). These contextual claims are well-supported by citations and general scientific knowledge.

results.result: Summary of main findings: CD31 localizes to the uropod with closed β2-integrins, is required for neutrophil polarization, and its absence prevents uropod detachment from ECM. Antagonizing integrin-ECM binding rescues the migration defect, while sustaining CD31 signaling enhances uropod detachment and migration. CD31 acts as a molecular rheostat controlling integrin-mediated adhesion at the uropod.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 summarize the main findings of the study. These summary claims are well-supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including microscopy (C92-C93), in vivo observations (C94), rescue experiments (C95), and gain-of-function studies (C96). The collective evidence from multiple experimental approaches provides strong support for these conclusions. These represent the core findings that advance understanding of CD31's role in neutrophil migration.
